messages.subject: Re: g.part 5 re-run
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sharmin,

to re-run with changed options you can either set overwrite = T, or simply delete the respective meta data. It is unlikely, that you would require to do this with regard to part1. I tend to delete the ms2-5 folders when re-running these parts.
To process all parts set mode=c(1,2,3,4,5).

Cheers,
David

Am Samstag, 29. Juni 2019 18:01:20 UTC+2 schrieb Sharmin:
> Hi David,
>
> Thank you very much for your feedback. I guess what's confusing me is how to re-run using any commands. I have my own script for the shell functions, and it loaded part 1 without any problems. It ran the whole file and started generating reports but stopped at part 2 only. Going back to re-run the shel from the cRAN script is a good way to start. Although it only specifies two modes, can I change that to 5? And should I use the meta directory to call the files or use the raw data files again? Creating a new output directory is a better idea and I already have created a new location. Sorry if these are redundant queries, but I'd like to know what you think, or how you would go about it?
>
> Thanks again!!
>
> Sharmin
>
> On Friday, June 28, 2019 at 11:28:53 AM UTC-4, David wrote:
> > Hi Sharmin,
> >
> > especially if you are new to GGIR I would recommend to use the shell function, it works best for me in any case. Maybe check out https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/vignettes/GGIR.html If everything is set up properly, it will skip all steps which have already been processed and add what was missing. You may want to consider to start over with an empty output directory.
> >
> > Good luck,
> > David
> >
> > Am Dienstag, 25. Juni 2019 22:56:42 UTC+2 schrieb Sharmin:
> > > Hi Everyone,
> > >
> > > I am very new to the GGIR package and related usage. Where I am stuck at the moment is to re-run my meta for parts 4 and  5 to get the summary files. For some reason, all the codes ran fine and started generating reports for part 2 as requested, but never went to part 4 and 5.
> > >
> > > I have the raw data files pre-processed already and all the meta files are available. Does anyone know what code I should use to re-do part.5? In the GGIR manual, part 4 with an overwrite function is available. But the next topic is g.plot instead of g.part5 (unless part 4 and part 5 essentially can use the same code listed). It would be really helpful to get some feedback!
> > >
> > >
> > > Thank you!
> > >
> > > Sharmin

messages.subject: Re: International workshop on statistical analyses for physical activity data in Granada (Spain)
messages.subject_clean: International workshop on statistical analyses for physical activity data in Granada (Spain)
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

Any application of accelerometer-derived physical activity data is welcome. Tests using different approaches to answer the same question are most welcome. But we expect a wide range of topics, from methodological aspects related to the measurement of physical activity itself to applications in different populations.

Best,
Jairo

El viernes, 28 de junio de 2019, 17:17:25 (UTC+2), David escribió:
> Hi Jairo,
>
> thanks a lot for organizing that workshop, it sounds fantastic.
> What kind of abstracts are you expecting? Any studies including activity data analyses or evaluations of different approaches with regard to statistics?
>
> Best regards,
> David
>
> Am Sonntag, 23. Juni 2019 11:27:39 UTC+2 schrieb Jairo Hidalgo Migueles:
> > Dear all,
> >
> > I am happy to tell you about the "International Workshop: a focus on statistical methods to analyse accelerometer-measured physical activity" (AIW2019) that we are going to host in Granada (Spain), the October 21st, 2019. Top experts will talk about compositional data analysis, multivariate pattern analysis and machine learning, the workshop will also include a hands-on session on accelerometer data processing with GGIR. More info and registrations here --> https://www.granadacongresos.com/aiw2019
> >
> > THE WORKSHOP
> > Objective instruments to measure physical activity are evolving at a drastic velocity. Recent developments have allowed to classify the accelerations produced by the human body as sleep, sedentary or physical activity time with a gradient of intensities. These categories of physical behaviour coexist in the 24 hours of the day with inter-relationships that classical statistical methods fail to consider. Researchers from all around the world are investigating how to overcome this limitation at analysing physical activity temporal series by using new statistical approaches such as isotemporal substitution models, compositional data analysis, multivariate pattern analysis with partial least squares regression and/or even machine learning algorithms.
> >
> > The present international workshop has been organized with the purpose of gathering together top experts from different countries in the abovementioned approaches to analyse physical activity data. This meeting will bring together different point of views on the state-of-the-art of physical activity data analysis, which will encourage interesting debates and, hopefully, will end up with practical recommendations on how to keep advancing to appropriately analyse physical activity data.
> >
> > We welcome all people interested in the topic to join us in Granada (Spain). All attendees will have the chance to send their abstract and present their studies as oral communications or posters during the workshop.
> >
> > I am happy to answer your related questions here or by email (jai...@ugr.es). Hope to see you in Granada!
> >
> > Best,
> > Jairo

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] GGIR Part 5 - save_ms5rawlevels=TRUE
messages.body_plain:
I have now implemented this in the master branch on GitHub and just uploaded a new release to CRAN. It should be available there in a couple of days.
The part5 csv output will then have an extra column with the names of the levels numbers to ease interpretation.
Thanks, Vincent

messages.subject: GGIR version 1.9-2 now online
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

GGIR release 1.9-2 is now online. Mostly minor updates as you can see in the change log <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/GGIR/news.html>.

Two updates may require a bit more clarification:

Argument 'ignorenonwear' is now set to TRUE by default. Previously, I set it to TRUE in my own work and also in the examples I gave in the vignette. However, if ignorenonwear was not provided by the user then GGIR used FALSE as a default. What does that mean: If it is TRUE then GGIR will not count non-wear periods towards sleep, even if they are imputed. The only scenario I can think of where you may want to set this to FALSE is if you know that the accelerometer was not worn during the night and if you want to force the analyses to treat all the non-wear time as sleep, or if you strongly believe that monitor non-wear always coincides with sleep.

Further, I have now made sure that argument 'def.noc.sleep' is set by default to use the HDCZA algorithm I added last year (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-31266-z) if no sleeplog is provided. In the example function calls in the vignette I already used it this way, but within GGIR it was not the default. This means that if you now use a sleeplog, GGIR will use the sleeplog first, if sleeplog is missing it will use the HDCZA algorithm, if the HDCZA algorithm for whatever reason fails to provide estimates then it used the L5 +/- 6 algorithm. If you use def.noc.sleep value c() and no sleeplog then L5 +/- 6 is used.

Previously, the HDCZA algorithm was only used if argument def.noc.sleep = 1 and if no sleeplog was provided.

Best wishes,

Vincent

messages.subject: Question regarding GGIR
messages.body_plain:
I would like to thank you for developing the GGIR package. It is an excellent R package, and we are using it to analyze our accelerometer data for subject with autism and their relatives. We have few questions and were wondering if you could provide any suggestions.

1. We are analyzing 21 days activity recorded using GeneActive watch. Let’s take an example. On a particular day, a person fall asleep at 10pm (based on raw data), woke up around midnight, fall asleep again at 2:57 am and finally woke up around 7 am. The GGRI algorithm identified the period between 2:57 am and 7 am as the time of “sleep onset” and “wake time” respectively. In another example where the person fall asleep at 10:46 pm, woke up at 3:42 am, again fall asleep at around 6 and finally woke up around 8am, the algorithm identified the 10:46 pm and 3:42 am as the “time of sleep onset” and “wake” respectively. So it seems the algorithm is identifying the maximum sleep duration and choosing the sleep onset and wake accordingly. However, in the examples we mentioned, we think the whole duration should be taken into consideration. Could you please suggest how to do that? The two plots are shown in the attached PPT (slide2). Many of our subjects have fragmented sleep and we would like to capture and analyze  this trait.

2. We also noticed that if a person falls asleep in the morning and sleeps past noon, the sleep offset would end at 11:59 am, and the rest of the sleep period past noon would be excluded from that night's sleep. Is there a way to include sleep past noon as part of the total sleep time? Please see attached PPT (slide4).

3. In our analysis, we only used the raw GeneActive data and did not include data from sleep diary.  In the GGIR output,  we got the value of the variables "sleeplog_onset", "sleeplog_wake" etc. We were wondering how the algorithm calculates the sleeplog time without any sleep diary data?

4. We were wondering what is the difference between "acc_n_noc" obtained in part 4 and "Nblocks_nightsleep_pla" obtained in part 5.

5. We were also wondering if the variable "Nblocks nightwak_and_IN30_pla" in part 5 provides the number of wake episodes during the sleep?

6. Does GGIR take into account daylight savings time?

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Question regarding GGIR
messages.body_plain:
Thanks Arpita, I believe we met on Skype and you are working in Pennsylvania. Nice to hear you are in the process of mastering GGIR.

1. Yes, the longest detected sleep period is used and I am aware that this is not ideal when people have fragmented sleep. Last year I listed <https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/issues/85> the detection of multiple periods as a possible area for improvement. However, to do this I need some form of support, either someone paying me for my time to do the work or someone doing the work instead of me and making a pull request. This is not a trivial addition, because we would carefully have to think how this is incorporated in the GGIR results. So, for the moment I prefer to postpone this work until there is a well defined project with enough time to work on this.
2. If a sleep diary (sleep log) is available then GGIR can handle the so called 'daysleepers' who go to bed before noon and wake up after noon. If no sleep diary is available then this does not work yet. I can implement this based on the same conditions as the previous point.
3. I initially developed the code for a study that has sleeplogs. Later on when I started to facilitate studies without sleeplogs I kept on using the term to refer to estimated sleep window times. I am aware that this can be confusing and I also listed <https://github.com/wadpac/GGIR/issues/162> the improvement of variable names as a possible area of future work.
4. They are almost identical. Part 5 first identifies segments in the day and then splits it up in days. Part 2 and 4 first split the time series and then perform the analysis per day. The order of identifying days and performing the analysis may have a minor influence on the values.
5. No, the definition is more narrow: the number of wake episodes with acceleration level 'inactive'.
6. Yes, GGIR takes into account daylight saving time.

Kind regards,
Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees
Independent consultant
www.movementdata.nl <http://www.movementdata.nl>

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] WASO
messages.body_plain:
Shouldn't that be: Total of all time use categories related to the night minus total sleep duration within the sleep period time window?
You do not need to discriminate between inactivity, moderate and vigorous activity for this. I would sum them and treat them together as wakefulness after sleep onset..
Needless to say that with wakefulness we actually mean 'more acceleration then in sleep', because an accelerometer does not directly measure the underlying neurological process of sleep and wake.
Vincent
